steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper showing that DNNs trained with a fixed random (ETF) classifier transfer better across domains. Motivate fixed classifiers through neural collapse, state what we study, list the contributions, and end with a short notation paragraph.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:

2. This paper: transferability of fixed ETF classifiers
3. Contributions
4. Notations

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Background
- DNNs revolutionized ML/pattern recognition; highly expressive feature extractors
- trend: fixed classifiers instead of trainable linear layers on top of last-layer features
- inspired by Neural Collapse (NC), late stages of training
- NC: last-layer features converge to class means, within-class variability -> zero, Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) geometry; last-layer classifiers match class activation means -> classifiers with ETF geometry

2. This paper
- transferability of DNNs trained with fixed ETF classifiers
- ETF implicitly enforces negligible within-class variability -> better cluster separability -> better transfer
- experiments: fine-grained image classification datasets, especially out-of-domain

3. Contributions
- Random Matrix Theory (RMT) results: linear random projector follows ETF classifier properties -> feature kernel with minimal class covariance
- empirical: fixed ETF classifiers -> better transfer on fine-grained datasets, esp. large domain shifts from source (Figure 1)
- compare: better than baselines training linear classifier from scratch (no covariance minimization) and SW (Switchable Whitening), which whitens feature covariance during training

4. Notations
- lowercase/uppercase boldface = vectors/matrices
- column vector / matrix with entries; ones vector; canonical class vector j_a; J

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) have changed machine learning and pattern recognition tasks a lot, because they give highly expressive feature extractors. A recent trend in training DNN models is to use fixed classifiers instead of the usual trainable linear layers on top of the features from the last layer of the DNNs. This idea comes from the Neural Collapse (NC) phenomenon, which happens during the late stages of model training. NC shows that the features from the last layer of the network converge to their class means, with the within-class variability collapsing to zero, and they form the so-called Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) geometry. The last-layer linear classifiers also match their class activation means perfectly, so the classifiers have ETF geometry too.

In this paper, we look at the transferability of DNN models trained with fixed classifiers that follow an ETF geometry. The ETF structure implicitly forces the within-class variability of features to be negligible, which makes the clusters more separable, and this improves transfer performance a lot. In our experiments we evaluate these models on various fine-grained image classification datasets, and especially on out-of-domain scenarios. Our contributions are:

[Contributions]
- RMT results: linear random projector follows ETF classifier properties -> feature kernel with minimal class covariance
- empirical: better transfer on fine-grained datasets, esp. large domain shifts (Figure 1)
- better than baselines training linear classifier from scratch (no covariance minimization) and SW (Switchable Whitening)

[Notations]
- boldface lowercase/uppercase = vectors/matrices; column vector and matrix with entries; ones vector; canonical class vector j_a; J

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) have changed machine learning and pattern recognition tasks a lot, because they give highly expressive feature extractors. A recent trend in training DNN models is to use fixed classifiers instead of the usual trainable linear layers on top of the features from the last layer of the DNNs. This idea comes from the Neural Collapse (NC) phenomenon, which happens during the late stages of model training. NC shows that the features from the last layer of the network converge to their class means, with the within-class variability collapsing to zero, and they form the so-called Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) geometry. The last-layer linear classifiers also match their class activation means perfectly, so the classifiers have ETF geometry too.

In this paper, we look at the transferability of DNN models trained with fixed classifiers that follow an ETF geometry. The ETF structure implicitly forces the within-class variability of features to be negligible, which makes the clusters more separable, and this improves transfer performance a lot. In our experiments we evaluate these models on various fine-grained image classification datasets, and especially on out-of-domain scenarios. Our contributions are:

- 1. Using existing results in Random Matrix Theory (RMT), we show that using a linear random projector follows the properties of ETF classifiers, which gives a feature kernel with minimal class covariance.

- 2. We then show empirically that DNNs trained with fixed ETF classifiers have better transfer performance on a range of fine-grained image classification datasets, especially on the ones with large domain shifts from the source dataset (see Figure 1).

- 3. We compare our approach with baseline methods that train the linear classifier from scratch (no covariance minimization), and with methods such as SW (Switchable Whitening) that explicitly whiten the feature covariance during training, and we show that our approach performs better.

Notations. We denote vectors by lowercase boldface letters and matrices by uppercase boldface letters. \left\{{\bf v}_{a}\right\}_{a=1}^{n} is the column vector {\bf v} with (scalar or vector) entries {\bf v}_{a}, and \left\{{\bf V}_{ab}\right\}_{a,b=1}^{n} is the matrix {\bf V} with (scalar or matrix) entries {\bf V}_{ab}. The vector {\bf 1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the column vector filled with ones. The vector {\bf j}_{a} is the canonical vector of class \mathcal{C}_{a}, defined by ({\bf j}_{a})_{i}=\delta_{{\bf x}_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{a}}, and {\bf J}=[{\bf j}_{1},\ldots,{\bf j}_{K}]\in\{0,1\}^{N\times K}.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) have revolutionized machine learning and pattern recognition tasks by providing highly expressive feature extractors. A recent trend in training DNN models is the use of fixed classifiers [1,2,3] instead of traditional trainable linear layers on top of features extracted from the last layer of the DNNs. This approach is inspired by the Neural Collapse (NC) phenomenon [4,5], which occurs during the late stages of model training. NC reveals that the features obtained from the last layer of the network converge to their class means, with within-class variability collapsing to zero, forming the so-called Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) geometry; the last-layer linear classifiers are perfectly matched with their class activation means, resulting in classifiers with ETF geometry.

In this paper, we explore the transferability of DNN models trained with fixed classifiers following an ETF geometry. The ETF structure implicitly enforces negligible within-class variability of features, which enhances cluster separability and in turn significantly improves transfer performance. Our experiments focus on evaluating these models on various fine-grained image classification datasets, especially in out-of-domain scenarios. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- 1. Using existing results in Random Matrix Theory (RMT), we establish that a linear random projector adheres to the properties of ETF classifiers, leading to a feature kernel with minimal class covariance.

- 2. We then empirically show that DNNs trained with fixed ETF classifiers lead to enhanced transfer performance on a range of fine-grained image classification datasets, especially on those with important domain shifts with respect to the source dataset (see Figure 1).

- 3. We show the superior performance of our approach compared with baseline methods that train the linear classifier from scratch (no covariance minimization), as well as methods such as SW (Switchable Whitening) [6] that explicitly perform feature covariance whitening during training.

Notations. Vectors (matrices) are denoted by lowercase (uppercase) boldface letters. \left\{{\bf v}_{a}\right\}_{a=1}^{n} is the column vector {\bf v} with (scalar or vector) entries {\bf v}_{a} and \left\{{\bf V}_{ab}\right\}_{a,b=1}^{n} is the matrix {\bf V} with (scalar or matrix) entries {\bf V}_{ab}. The vector {\bf 1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} stands for the column vector filled with ones. The vector {\bf j}_{a} is the canonical vector of class \mathcal{C}_{a}, defined by ({\bf j}_{a})_{i}=\delta_{{\bf x}_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{a}}, and {\bf J}=[{\bf j}_{1},\ldots,{\bf j}_{K}]\in\{0,1\}^{N\times K}.

References:
[1] Jianfeng Lu and Stefan Steinerberger, “Neural collapse with cross-entropy loss,” arXiv:2012.08465 , 2020.
[2] Yibo Yang, Shixiang Chen, Xiangtai Li, Liang Xie, Lin Zhouchen, and Dacheng Tao, “Inducing neural collapse in imbalanced learning: Do we really need a learnable classifier at the end of deep neural network,” NeurIPS , vol. 35, pp. 37991–38002, 2022.
[3] Yibo Yang, Haobo Yuan, Xiangtai Li, Zhouchen Lin, Philip Torr, and Dacheng Tao, “Neural collapse inspired feature-classifier alignment for few-shot class incremental learning,” arXiv:2302.03004 , 2023.
[4] Vardan Papyan, XY Han, and David L Donoho, “Prevalence of neural collapse during the terminal phase of deep learning training,” PNAS , vol. 117, no. 40, pp. 24652–24663, 2020.
[5] Peifeng Gao, Qianqian Xu, Peisong Wen, Huiyang Shao, Zhiyong Yang, and Qingming Huang, “A study of neural collapse phenomenon: Grassmannian frame, symmetry, generalization,” arXiv:2304.08914 , 2023.
[6] Xingang Pan, Xiaohang Zhan, Jianping Shi, Xiaoou Tang, and Ping Luo, “Switchable whitening for deep representation learning,” in Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision , 2019, pp. 1863–1871.
